summary: Argues against the notion that TCP is unsuitable for local area networks. It was originally published by MITRE.

eli5.summary: Some people thought TCP was too heavy for a small local network. This memo says that is not so.

what is the difference between tcp and ip

subtitle: A position paper arguing that fear of running TCP on a local network is a Woozle: a scare built on misunderstanding.

tldr.problem: Some people held that TCP and IP are too heavy for a Local Area Network, which has high bit rates and low error rates.
tldr.mechanism: The author defines what a LAN, TCP and IP actually are, shows that layers are not monoliths, and argues that TCP is needed to talk to the wider internet anyway.
tldr.outcome: The paper concludes that the fear of using TCP on a local net is unfounded. It is a position paper, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 872 is an Informational position paper from September 1982, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is best read as a record of the 1982 argument rather than as a specification; see RFC 793 for TCP itself.

sections.title: The Woozle Thesis
sections.content:
RFC 872, by M.A. Padlipsky of The MITRE Corporation, argues that fearing TCP-on-a-LAN is a Woozle which needs slaying. A Woozle, borrowed from Winnie-the-Pooh, is an imaginary beast: Pooh and Piglet follow tracks, convince each other it is a herd of Hostile Animals, and then find they were following their own tracks.

The author's contention is that the expressed fears come from misunderstanding the protocol and the environment, not from the technical facts. To settle it, the paper asks three things: what is a Woozle, what is a LAN, and what is a TCP.
sections.eli5: It is like chasing footprints and being scared of a monster, only to find the footprints were yours all along.

sections.title: What a LAN Really Is
sections.content:
The paper describes a LAN as a communications subnetwork for relatively short distances (typically a few kilometers), at relatively high bit rates (typically greater than a few hundred kilobits per second) with relatively low error rates. Its hosts are, at least in principle, heterogeneous and talk through layered protocols.

Two things are ruled out. A processor-to-processor bus is likely a closely coupled distributed processor or a loosely coupled multiprocessor, not a LAN. A system that only lets terminals reach different hosts, with no intercomputer networking protocols between them, is a Localized Communications Network (LCN), not the kind of LAN the paper means.

The paper notes that high capacity and good error properties lead some to say such a medium does not need a heavy-duty protocol designed for long-haul nets. It adds that the assumption of resource-sharing protocols between hosts is just as significant.
sections.eli5: A LAN is a neighborhood road where different kinds of computers chat using agreed rules. A single computer's inside wiring is not a neighborhood road.

sections.title: TCP, IP and UDP in Layers
sections.content:
TCP is a host-to-host protocol. Its most significant property is that it presents reliable logical connections to protocols above it. It is also designed for a "catenet" (an internet), so it addresses a foreign host as a foreign net plus a foreign host.

That addressing means TCP needs an adjunct to deal with the proximate net, which is the Internet Protocol (IP). IP was made a separate protocol so other host-to-host protocols can use it too. It maps generic network qualities such as precedence, grade of service and security labeling to the closest equivalent on the local net, decides whether an address is on the proximate net or must go to a gateway, fragments and reassembles packets, and identifies the calling protocol so the receiver can demultiplex.

The paper also points out UDP, designed for speed rather than accuracy. If all you want is to tell data streams apart, UDP will do, and packetized speech is the usual example. The moral of the paper's two figures is that in ARPANET-style layering, layers are not monoliths.
sections.eli5: TCP is the careful delivery person, IP is the map that finds the right street, and UDP is a quick note thrown over the fence.

sections.title: Why TCP Still Makes Sense Locally
sections.content:
If you are talking to a host out on the catenet, you use IP. If your application wants reliable, flow-controlled, ordered delivery over logical connections addressed through a Well-Known Socket, you use TCP above IP, whether or not the other host is on your own net. If the application does not need TCP's properties, do not use it, wherever you are. You can even skip IP for local hosts, though that may make implementation messy.

The paper cautions that such applications will probably need some host-to-host protocol anyway, and keeping parallel protocol suites is a nuisance. Since TCP is needed to reach the catenet, it is usually better to use it locally as well.

On the checksum, the author first thought it was overkill on a LAN. Metering of TCP implementations on several host types showed that checksum processing took only around 12% of per-transmission processing time, so an alternate local protocol is hard to justify.
sections.eli5: Using one set of rules for both nearby and faraway friends is easier than learning two. The extra checking only costs a little time anyway.

sections.title: Other Properties and Speed Claims
sections.content:
The paper lists further points in TCP/IP's favor: protocol interpreters exist for a dozen or two operating systems, the protocols have worked for several years, and IP puts no constraints on the interface presented by the proximate net or on its users. It notes that, unlike X.25, IP can take advantage of alternate routing. Both TCP/IP are Department of Defense Standards, and virtual terminal and file transfer protocols compatible with them exist.

On speed, the research community had reported rates in excess of 300 kb/s on an 800 kb/s subnet, 1.2 Mb/s on a 3 Mb/s subnet, and 9.2 kb/s on a 9.6 kb/s phone line, all using TCP.

A worked example looks at the PDSC system. With 16 kb screen loads, 17 ms average disk latency, about 2 ms per context switch and 1 ms for transmission, a host could present only 50 screens per second, which is 800 kb/s. That is well within TCP-achievable rates, so hosts may not be able to supply enough bits to overtax the protocols. The author still calls for careful measurement of TCP/IP performance on a LAN.
sections.eli5: People had already timed TCP and it ran quickly. Even a busy computer cannot hand over information fast enough to make TCP the slow part.
